cards.text: Paul, the apostle writing this letter, is teaching the church in Corinth about spiritual gifts. He just told them to eagerly desire the greater gifts, and then he said: "And now I will show you the most excellent way." Friend, that's a cliffhanger, and I'm leaning in like it's the oven door on a fresh batch.
Paul starts with himself: what if he could speak in the tongues of men and of angels? Friend, that's not bilingual. That's HEAVEN-lingual.

cards.question: Paul speaks in the tongues of men and of angels, but he has no love. What does he say he is?

answers.text: A ringing gong or a clanging cymbal

cards.text: Then Paul cranks it up: the gift of prophecy, all mysteries, all knowledge, and faith so big it moves mountains. MOUNTAINS! I need my whole mustache just to move a bowl of dough.

cards.question: Prophecy, all knowledge and mountain-moving faith, but no love. What does Paul say he is?

cards.text: Then Paul goes all in. He gives all he possesses to the poor, and he even exults in the surrender of his body.

cards.question: Paul says if he gives all he possesses to the poor but has no love, he still gains nothing.

cards.text: Gaining nothing? Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer, I could TEACH that class. Now Paul turns to what love looks like: "Love is patient, love is kind."

cards.question: Love is patient and kind. So when someone else gets the bigger blessing, what does love do?

cards.text: Love doesn't boast, it isn't proud, it isn't rude, and it isn't self-seeking. Meanwhile, the day my edges came back sharp, I stamped one perfect cookie and showed it to every oven in the bakery. TWICE.

cards.question: Paul says love is easily angered, as long as it cools off quickly.
Somebody does you dirty. Paul says love keeps no account of ___.

cards.text: No spreadsheet of wrongs. No color coding. No TABS. And Paul keeps going: love takes no pleasure in evil.

cards.question: Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the ___.

cards.text: Next, Paul says love bears all things. ALL things, friend, even the coworker who hits reply-all on the whole company.

cards.question: Love bears all things. Paul says it believes all things and hopes all things, but endures only some things.

cards.text: Then Paul says it plain: "Love never fails." Now he sets love right next to those big gifts: prophecies, tongues and knowledge.

cards.question: Love never fails. What does Paul say happens to prophecies, tongues and knowledge?

cards.text: Paul says why: right now we know in part and we prophesy in part. It's like peeking at a batch through the oven window, something's happening in there, but is it DONE? No clue.

cards.question: We know in part. But when the perfect comes, the ___ passes away.

cards.text: Then Paul gets personal: when he was a child, he talked, thought and reasoned like a child. Me? My first week on the Millers' counter, every time the oven timer went off, I was SURE the kitchen was on fire.

cards.question: When Paul became a man, he held on to his childish ways.

cards.text: Now Paul says we see but a dim reflection, as in a mirror. Like trying to read a text with the sun blasting your phone screen.

cards.question: Right now it's a dim reflection. How does Paul say we shall see then?
Paul knows in part now, but he says one day he will know fully, even as he is fully known.

cards.text: Then Paul lands the whole thing, quiet and steady. Three things remain.

cards.question: Paul says three things remain. Which three?
Faith, hope and love remain. But Paul says the greatest of these is ___.

cards.text: Hold that thought, friend. Paul's not done teaching on these gifts, so keep your apron on.

findings.problem: The card says Paul is the apostle writing this letter to the church in Corinth, and that he is teaching about spiritual gifts. These facts come from outside the passage (1 Corinthians 1:1-2 and 12:1), but the card cites only 1 Corinthians 12:31.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The question drops Paul's "If" and states it as fact: "Paul speaks in the tongues of men and of angels, but he has no love." Verse 1 is a hypothetical ("If I speak... but have not love").

The card states as fact that Paul gives all he possesses to the poor and exults in the surrender of his body ("Then Paul goes all in. He gives all he possesses..."). Verse 3 is a hypothetical ("If I give all I possess...").

The joke compares verse 3 (giving away everything, even your body, yet gaining nothing without love) to Papa Dorin sitting idle in a junk drawer. Those are different actions: giving everything versus sitting forgotten. So the comparison doesn't click for verse 3.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The fill-in-the-blank asks the baker to finish the wording of verse 6 ("rejoices in the ___": truth, victory or reward). Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason their way to "truth" over the other two. It is guessing the next word of the line.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The question covers three groups, and the right answer is "They come to an end." In the BSB, prophecies "will cease" and knowledge "will be dismissed," but tongues "will be restrained." Restrained is not clearly the same as coming to an end, so the answer may not be true for every group.

rule.text: A card about two groups needs an answer true for both.

findings.problem: The joke adds a new moment to Papa Dorin's backstory: his first week on the Millers' counter, thinking the kitchen was on fire every time the oven timer went off. This is a made-up moment in the Millers' kitchen, not around his bakery.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The last story card only says the teaching isn't over. It tells nothing from the passage, but it cites 1 Corinthians 13:13. The docs allow a final card that is just this line, but they don't say what such a card should cite.
findings.question: What should the verses field be on a final story card that only says the story or teaching isn't over and tells no verse? Should it be the passage's last verse, null, or something else?
